findings.finding: test_release_e2e_cli.py named TOKEN like test_rollback_e2e_cli.py's token-leak guard but never asserted it. Fixed: added TOKEN-not-in-stdout/stderr assertions to the confirm-and-deploy and auto-rollback E2E tests.

_client()/_hosting_errors() duplicated from rollback.py instead of extracted, contradicting this same diff's own 'one oracle' rationale for test_gate.py. Fixed: extracted to new hosting.py, both rollback.py and release.py import from there.

deploy_from_git failure path was untested and multiplexed into the same exit code/reason shape as a smoke failure. Fixed: added failure_stage field (deploy/smoke/smoke_config), renamed EXIT_SMOKE_FAILED to EXIT_NOT_RELEASED, added test_a_deploy_failure_is_reported_not_raised.
release() did five things in one function.
redundant canonical_ref() re-application on an already-canonical previous_ref.
import placement in release.py did not actually match rollback.py's own convention despite claiming to.
run_smoke_test/smoke_policy ValueError/ProfileError for bad --smoke-* flags was uncaught, crashing with a traceback instead of a structured result.
jelastic_client.deploy_from_git never re-pins the branch for an already-existing VCS project (pre-existing, out of scope for this diff).

Claim under doubt: Auto-rollback restores the previously-live ref, undoing a bad release. — jelastic_client.deploy_from_git (pre-existing, unmodified by this unit) never re-pins the branch for an environment that already has a VCS project — it only sends `branch` on first-ever creation. On the routine 'push new commits to the same branch, CI redeploys' cycle, previous_ref already equals the branch being deployed, so auto-rollback has no distinct commit to name and cannot actually undo the new commits that broke the deploy.
findings.suggestion: Either implement commit-level rollback (a versioning/tagging scheme) or document the branch-name-granularity limitation so operators know when auto-rollback has nothing to restore.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: A failed smoke check reliably indicates the release is unhealthy and should trigger an auto-rollback. — With no polling deadline configured (neither --profile nor --smoke-max-wait), smoke_test.py makes exactly one fixed-timeout attempt — its own docstring warns 'a fifteen-second start-up gets reported as a failed release and triggers a rollback nobody needed'. A single attempt is not a reliable enough signal to justify an automatic host mutation.
findings.suggestion: Skip auto-rollback (with a clear reason) unless a polling deadline was actually configured, since only then has the smoke check given the app a real chance to come up.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: release.py is safe to wire into an automated CI pipeline without additional guardrails. — Nothing in release()'s original signature distinguished dev from prod. A CI job configured with a PROD env_name would perform an auto-rollback-capable PROD deploy with zero human confirmation, violating the constitution's PROD-is-ASK-FIRST invariant, which this agent-free entry point has no built-in way to honour (it cannot show an AskUserQuestion).
findings.suggestion: Require an explicit target argument with no default, and refuse target=prod unless an explicit confirm_prod flag (sourced from something upstream that can actually ask a human) is set.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: release.py can be safely invoked from CI for every push without additional coordination. — There is no lock across the whole gate->deploy->smoke->rollback sequence. Two concurrent release.py invocations against the same env_name could interleave their deploy/rollback calls, each unaware of the other's in-flight mutation.
findings.suggestion: Add a per-env_name lock spanning the whole sequence, or explicitly document that callers must serialize releases per environment upstream.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: A rollback_triggered: true result with rollback.success: true means the environment is healthy again. — rollback_git only confirms the ref PIN was accepted (or, at best, read back as matching) — it does not itself confirm the application is actually serving traffic on that ref. Nothing in the reported payload distinguished 'restored to a known-good ref' from 'restored to an unverified ref that still isn't answering requests'.
findings.suggestion: Re-run the smoke check against the restored ref after a successful rollback and surface the result distinctly from the pin confirmation.

findings.finding: Claim under doubt: The rollback_skipped_reason 'no distinct previous ref to restore — nothing to roll back to' accurately communicates the situation to an operator. — That wording reads as reassuring — as if there truly is nothing to restore — when it is actually surfacing the branch-vs-commit granularity gap (finding #1): a live regression from this deploy's own new commits could still be unrestored, because auto-rollback only sees branch names, not commits.
findings.suggestion: Reword the message to name the actual gap instead of implying nothing was missed.
